source.title: Limits to Depth Efﬁciencies of Self-Attention Supplementary Material
source.authors: Yoav Levine; Noam Wies; Or Sharir; Hofit Bata; A. Shashua

record.file_problem: The text is a full paper with supplementary appendices; the supplied title calls it supplementary material. The text is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper’s own architecture sweeps compare depth and width at matched parameter budgets and report that the better-performing depth changes with network size. This refines and challenges the claim that architecture details have only a slight effect.
record.gate_note: The paper tests depth–width allocation and held-out language-model loss, not power-law loss scaling, small-run extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, other modalities or regimes, or downstream predictability. Its discussion of Kaplan et al. and the reproduced Kaplan figure are cited results, not this study’s results. Figures 2–3 and Table 1 report architecture comparisons and projections, but Table 1’s projections are not loss measurements.
record.test_reason: The study trains decoder-only LMs at depths 6 to 48 at matched parameter counts (10^6 to 6·10^8). It reports held-out loss differences between depths that are statistically significant and change sign with size. It argues explicitly against Kaplan et al.'s reading that depth-to-width ratio barely matters. This is a result and a specific argument that V4 needs restating.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that self-attention has a width-dependent transition between depth-inefficiency and depth-efficiency. At fixed size, a network can be too shallow or too deep, so Kaplan et al.'s 'depth inefficiency' holds only in one regime. They provide fitted guidelines for the optimal depth-to-width ratio, projecting GPT-3 175B as too deep and about 30K width as optimal for 1T parameters.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies depth–width allocation in decoder-only self-attention language models, using held-out loss and matched-parameter-budget architecture comparisons; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative loss of deeper and shallower models changes with network size and width; the transition width depends on depth.

fits_no_version.finding: The transition width at which a deeper net becomes better grows exponentially with depth. The fit is log dx = 5.039 + 0.0555·L (R²=0.998, χ²red=0.854, 5 points), with an implied optimal-depth-per-size curve.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-optimal depth-to-width ratio at fixed parameter count follows a predictable size-dependent law (optimal depth grows logarithmically with width).

fits_no_version.finding: The fit is extrapolated to project that GPT-3 175B is too deep (optimal L≈80) and that a 1T model should have width about 30K (Table 1, Fig 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Projected optimal architecture shapes for large LMs; these are not measurements.

record.problems: The empirical sweep is restricted to decoder-only models trained on English Wikipedia, BookCorpus and OpenWebText, with vocabulary size 2000 and network sizes between 10^6 and 6 · 10^8 parameters. The numerical loss values for the depth comparisons are shown in figures rather than stated in the text; the text gives qualitative outcomes. The theoretical analysis removes activations and normalizations, though the empirical experiments include them.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the transition-width fit or GPT-3 architecture projections: these concern optimal depth–width allocation, not a version’s named loss-scaling, compute-optimal parameter/token, or downstream outcome. Numerical architecture and loss values in Figure 2 were not assigned from the figure.

untested.parts: Power-law loss in parameters, tokens or compute; no such fit is reported.
Extrapolation of loss from small runs. The extrapolation done concerns the optimal depth per size, not loss.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; tokens are fixed (1M steps × 512 × 128).
Architecture details other than depth versus width. Heads are fixed at 2, and feed-forward ratio and attention dimension are not varied.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting or setup choices.

missing.what: Width-efficiency regime: at small sizes, deeper nets perform worse than shallower nets of the same size.
Best-performing depth per size range among L=6,12,24,48.
Run-to-run std of test loss (6.5e-4 to 2.1e-3). This is needed to judge whether the significant depth gaps are small.
Estimated transition widths per depth (e.g. L=6: 214, L=30: 824).

record.verdict_notes: The rows split each depth comparison into duplicate shallow and deep members, all marked 'reversed'. Since V4 is a magnitude claim and every loss value is figure-only, the states are set to cannot_determine. The verdict rests on the text: statistically significant, sign-changing depth effects at matched size. The reproduced Kaplan Fig 1(a) is a cited result and is correctly excluded. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out loss in parameters, tokens or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-budget-optimal growth of parameter and token counts; the study instead examines depth and width at fixed parameter budgets.
The paper tests depth and width effects at matched parameter budgets, but does not systematically test every other architecture detail or quantify their effect across a broad range.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.

Whether scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on setup or fitting choices, and whether scaling-law curves bend. The paper fits an exponential depth–width transition, not the scaling laws described in this version.

relationships.condition: Decoder-only LMs, 10^6 to 6·10^8 non-embedding params, depths 6 to 48, matched parameter budgets
relationships.reason: At fixed size, held-out loss differs significantly between depths, and the best depth shifts with size. Shallower wins at small sizes and deeper wins after widening (R1–R12, Fig 2, Fig 3(c)). So shape is not irrelevant, but the gap magnitudes are figure-only and can't be shown to be large.
relationships.display_finding: Held-out loss differed significantly across depths at fixed size, with shallower models winning at small sizes and deeper models winning after widening.

source_check.condition: Decoder-only LMs, 10^6 to 6·10^8 non-embedding params, depths 6 to 48, matched parameter budgets
source_check.reason: R1–R12 and Sections 5.2.1–5.2.3 establish size-dependent depth preferences, including shallower advantages at small sizes and deeper advantages after widening. This qualifies shape insensitivity; unreported numerical loss gaps prevent concluding that changes exceed V4's slight-effect allowance.

relation.reason: The study directly compares held-out language-model loss across depths and widths at matched parameter budgets.

tranche.reason: Matched-budget experiments and an explicit argument qualify architectural insensitivity by showing width-dependent depth efficiency and size-dependent preferred depth.

source_check.notes: The twelve rows represent six paired comparisons, not twelve independent results; numerical loss gaps are unavailable in the extracted text. The supplied text is titled The Depth-to-Width Interplay in Self-Attention, arXiv v3 dated January 2021, and includes the main paper and appendices.
